subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is the function of the non-conducting (fibrous) tissue between the atria and ventricles?
options: To speed conduction directly from atria to ventricles
To prevent blood entering the ventricles
To act as a second pacemaker
To delay and channel the impulse through the AVN so the ventricles contract after the atria
questions.explain: The fibrous ring stops the impulse passing directly to the ventricles, forcing it through the AVN, ensuring atria empty before ventricles contract.

questions.q: A non-competitive inhibitor that binds reversibly to an allosteric site will, on a rate-against-substrate graph, produce:
options: a reduced Km and unchanged Vmax
no change to either value
an unchanged Km but a reduced Vmax
an increased Vmax
questions.explain: Because substrate binding is unaffected, Km stays the same, but fewer functional enzymes mean a lower maximum rate, so Vmax falls.

questions.q: In an enzyme-catalysed reaction, doubling the enzyme concentration while keeping substrate in large excess will:
options: cause denaturation
have no effect on the initial rate
halve the rate
approximately double the initial rate of reaction
questions.explain: With excess substrate, the number of available active sites limits the rate, so doubling enzyme concentration roughly doubles the rate.

questions.q: On a rate-against-substrate-concentration graph, increasing the concentration of a COMPETITIVE inhibitor would:
options: lower the Vmax that can be reached
have no effect on the curve
prevent Vmax ever being reached even at infinite substrate
increase the substrate concentration needed to reach the same rate, but Vmax is still attainable
questions.explain: Competitive inhibition can be overcome by sufficient substrate, so Vmax is unchanged but more substrate is needed to approach it.

questions.q: Below the optimum temperature, the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction is low mainly because:
options: substrate and enzyme molecules have less kinetic energy, so successful collisions forming complexes are less frequent
the activation energy has increased
the enzyme is denatured
the active site has changed shape permanently
questions.explain: At lower temperatures molecules move more slowly, reducing the frequency of effective collisions and the formation of enzyme-substrate complexes.

questions.q: Spongy mesophyll in a leaf is adapted for gas exchange because:
options: It transports water to the stomata
It actively pumps carbon dioxide into the cells
It contains many chloroplasts for trapping light
Air spaces between loosely packed cells provide a large moist surface for diffusion
questions.explain: Loosely packed cells with interconnected air spaces give a large moist surface area, allowing gases to diffuse to and from photosynthesising cells.

questions.q: Guard cells open the stomata when they:
options: Lose water and become flaccid
Accumulate solutes, take up water by osmosis and become turgid
Lose potassium ions to neighbouring cells
Are exposed to darkness
questions.explain: Active uptake of K+ lowers guard-cell water potential, so water enters by osmosis; the cells become turgid and bend apart, opening the pore.

questions.q: Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion in that it:
options: uses channel or carrier proteins to move polar/charged molecules down their gradient
moves substances against their concentration gradient
requires ATP
only occurs across the nuclear envelope
questions.explain: Facilitated diffusion is passive but uses transport proteins to allow polar or charged molecules to cross the hydrophobic bilayer, still down the gradient.

questions.q: Which factor would DECREASE the rate of transpiration from a leaf?
options: A decrease in atmospheric humidity
An increase in air movement (wind)
An increase in atmospheric humidity
A rise in temperature
questions.explain: Higher humidity reduces the water-potential gradient between the leaf air spaces and the atmosphere, slowing diffusion of water vapour out.

questions.q: An irreversible inhibitor such as a heavy metal ion binding to a sulfhydryl group at the active site would be classified by its mechanism as broadly:
options: an inhibitor that permanently alters the enzyme so activity is not restored by adding substrate
a competitive inhibitor that can be reversed by adding substrate
a coenzyme
an activator that increases Vmax
questions.explain: Irreversible inhibitors bind so strongly (often covalently) that activity cannot be restored simply by increasing substrate concentration.

questions.q: Which factor would increase the permeability of a cell membrane?
options: Removal of all membrane proteins
Increasing cholesterol content
A decrease in temperature, increasing phospholipid order
An increase in temperature, increasing phospholipid movement and creating gaps
questions.explain: Higher temperatures increase phospholipid kinetic energy and fluidity, and can denature membrane proteins, increasing permeability.

questions.q: A change in pH away from the optimum reduces enzyme activity because:
options: it increases the kinetic energy of the substrate
H+ or OH- ions disrupt ionic and hydrogen bonds, altering active site shape
it lowers the activation energy
it permanently increases enzyme concentration
questions.explain: Changes in pH alter charges on R-groups and disrupt bonds maintaining the tertiary structure, distorting the active site.

questions.q: During ventricular systole, the atrioventricular valves close because:
options: The semilunar valves are open
Atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure
Ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure
The ventricles are relaxing and filling
questions.explain: As the ventricles contract their pressure rises above that of the atria, forcing the AV valves shut to prevent backflow.

questions.q: The wall of the left ventricle is thicker than that of the right ventricle because it must:
options: Hold a larger volume of blood
Generate a higher pressure to force blood around the entire systemic circulation
Contract more slowly than the right ventricle
Pump blood only to the nearby lungs
questions.explain: The left ventricle pumps blood through the high-resistance systemic circuit, requiring more cardiac muscle to generate greater pressure.

questions.q: Why does an enzyme show specificity for a particular substrate?
options: because all enzymes catalyse every reaction
because the substrate has the same primary structure as the enzyme
because the enzyme provides activation energy to all molecules equally
because the precise 3D shape of the active site, determined by tertiary structure, is complementary to one substrate
questions.explain: The active site's specific shape, arising from the protein's folding, is complementary only to a particular substrate, conferring specificity.

questions.q: On a Michaelis-Menten curve, the Km value of an enzyme represents the substrate concentration at which:
options: all active sites are denatured
the reaction rate is half of Vmax
the reaction stops completely
the enzyme concentration is zero
questions.explain: Km is the substrate concentration giving half the maximum rate; a low Km indicates a high affinity of the enzyme for its substrate.

questions.q: Ringing experiments, in which a ring of bark (and phloem) is removed from a tree trunk, support the role of phloem in translocation because:
options: Sugars accumulate in the bulge above the ring while tissues below may die
The xylem also stops functioning
Water stops reaching the leaves above the ring
The leaves immediately wilt
questions.explain: Sugars cannot pass the removed phloem, so they build up above the ring, showing phloem carries organic solutes.

questions.q: End-product inhibition, a form of metabolic control, typically operates because the end product acts as a:
options: non-competitive (allosteric) inhibitor of an enzyme earlier in the pathway
coenzyme for the first enzyme
competitive inhibitor of the final enzyme
substrate for the first reaction
questions.explain: The end product binds allosterically to an early enzyme, reducing its activity and preventing wasteful overproduction; this is negative feedback.

questions.q: Enzymes increase the rate of reaction by:
options: being permanently changed by the reaction
increasing the activation energy of the reaction
raising the temperature of the substrate
lowering the activation energy by providing an alternative reaction pathway
questions.explain: Enzymes lower the activation energy required, allowing more substrate molecules to react at a given temperature.

questions.q: A flatworm relies on diffusion across its body surface for gas exchange. Which feature of its body makes this possible despite having no specialised system?
options: A flattened shape giving a large surface area and short diffusion distance to all cells
A closed circulatory system carrying haemoglobin
A high metabolic rate requiring rapid oxygen delivery
A thick, impermeable cuticle
questions.explain: Its flat, thin body provides a large SA:V ratio and ensures no cell is far from the surface, so diffusion alone suffices.

questions.q: The sino-atrial node (SAN) is described as the pacemaker of the heart because it:
options: Prevents the atria and ventricles from contracting together
Initiates waves of excitation that set the basic heart rate
Receives blood from the vena cava
Conducts the impulse to the ventricles after a delay
questions.explain: The SAN spontaneously generates waves of depolarisation that spread across the atria and set the heart's intrinsic rhythm.

questions.q: The chloride shift refers to:
options: The movement of Cl- into red blood cells to balance the charge as HCO3- leaves
The loss of Cl- from plasma during digestion
The active uptake of chloride during the Bohr effect
The exchange of oxygen for chloride at the alveoli
questions.explain: As hydrogencarbonate ions diffuse out of red cells, chloride ions move in to maintain electrical neutrality.

questions.q: In phloem, the mass-flow hypothesis explains translocation as a result of:
options: Capillary action in the sieve tubes
Diffusion of sucrose from source to sink
Cohesion-tension pulling sap upward
Active loading of sucrose at the source lowering water potential, drawing in water and raising hydrostatic pressure that drives flow to the sink
questions.explain: Sucrose loaded at the source lowers water potential so water enters by osmosis, raising pressure and forcing sap toward sinks where sucrose is unloaded.

questions.q: A prosthetic group differs from a coenzyme in that a prosthetic group is:
options: always an inorganic metal ion in solution
a temporarily bound vitamin derivative
the substrate of the reaction
a permanently and tightly bound non-protein component of the enzyme
questions.explain: A prosthetic group is permanently bound to the enzyme (e.g. FAD in some dehydrogenases), unlike a coenzyme which associates only transiently.

questions.q: In a fish gill, the counter-current flow of water and blood is efficient because:
options: Water flows faster than blood, reversing the gradient
It allows carbon dioxide to be reabsorbed into the blood
A diffusion gradient for oxygen is maintained across the entire length of the lamella
Blood and water flow in the same direction, equalising oxygen quickly
questions.explain: Counter-current flow keeps the oxygen concentration of water higher than that of blood along the whole gill lamella, maintaining a diffusion gradient throughout.

questions.q: The Bohr effect describes how an increase in carbon dioxide (and fall in pH):
options: Has no effect on oxygen affinity
Increases the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
Shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, so haemoglobin releases more oxygen at a given partial pressure
Shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the left, increasing haemoglobin's affinity
questions.explain: Higher CO2 lowers haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, shifting the curve right so more oxygen is unloaded in respiring tissues.

questions.q: The semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves open when:
options: Atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure
The AV valves are also open
The ventricles relax during diastole
Ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the aorta and pulmonary artery
questions.explain: Once ventricular pressure rises above arterial pressure the semilunar valves open and blood is ejected.

questions.q: During atrial systole, blood moves from the atria into the ventricles because:
options: The semilunar valves open
Ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure
The atria relax and fill with blood
Atrial pressure rises above ventricular pressure, pushing the AV valves open
questions.explain: Contraction of the atria raises atrial pressure above that of the ventricles, forcing the open AV valves to allow blood through.

questions.q: In the human gas-exchange system, which sequence correctly lists the path of air during inspiration?
options: Bronchi, trachea, bronchioles, alveoli
Bronchioles, bronchi, trachea, alveoli
Trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli
Trachea, bronchioles, bronchi, alveoli
questions.explain: Air passes from the trachea to the bronchi, then the finer bronchioles, and finally reaches the alveoli where exchange occurs.

questions.q: On a graph of reaction rate against temperature for a human enzyme, the rate rises to a peak around 37 C then falls sharply. The sharp fall above 40 C is best explained by:
options: an increase in enzyme concentration
a fall in substrate concentration
a continued increase in kinetic energy
denaturation as bonds maintaining the active site break
questions.explain: Beyond the optimum, excessive vibration breaks the hydrogen and ionic bonds holding the tertiary structure, denaturing the active site and sharply reducing activity.
